document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 9(1)-(9) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Risk management system
responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
applicability: High-risk AI systems (classified under Art. 6 and Annexes I/III). Risks covered are limited to those that can be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through development, design or adequate technical information (Art. 9(3)). Art. 9(9) requires consideration of impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups.
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).
exact_text: A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.
verification_notes: Binding requirement. The article is phrased in the passive voice; the duty-holder (provider) is established through Art. 16(a) and the reference to 'providers' in Art. 9(9). OVERLAP: Art. 9(6)-(8) (OJ p. 57) also imposes testing duties (testing against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds, before market placement) that fit Safety and Testing; coded here under Risk Assessment only, to avoid double counting, with the testing element noted. Art. 9(10) (integration with risk procedures under other Union law, e.g. financial services) is outside the coded range. No amendment marker (M1) appears in Art. 9 of the consolidated text; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128; OJ p. 123) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 10(1)-(4), (6) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Data and data governance; read with Article 4a(1)
responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
applicability: High-risk AI systems that use techniques involving the training of AI models with data. For high-risk systems not using such training techniques, paras 2, 3 and 4 and Art. 4a(1) apply only to testing data sets (Art. 10(6) as amended).
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).
exact_text: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
verification_notes: CODING DECISION: Art. 10 is fundamentally a data governance provision, even though some of its requirements relate to risk mitigation. It is coded under Risk Assessment for now because its core operative elements, bias examination (Art. 10(2)(f)), bias detection, prevention and mitigation (Art. 10(2)(g)) and identification of data gaps (Art. 10(2)(h)), are risk identification and mitigation functions. Secondary dimension: Data Governance (see secondary_dimension; candidate sixth dimension for the codebook). A further link to Safety and Testing (quality of testing data sets) is noted but not coded. Single record, no double count. AMENDMENT: Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 amended Art. 10(1) (M1 marker) so the quality criteria now refer to paras 2, 3 and 4 and to Art. 4a(1) instead of paras 2 to 5. It also deleted Art. 10(5) and moved the special-category data rule into new Art. 4a (cons. p. 12). The coded exact_text (opening of Art. 10(2)) appears unamended. PERMISSION vs OBLIGATION: Art. 4a(1) PERMITS providers of high-risk AI systems, exceptionally and where strictly necessary, to process special categories of personal data for the bias detection and correction required by Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), subject to cumulative safeguards. Art. 4a(2) extends that permission to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models and to deployers of high-risk systems, and expressly states that it does not create any obligation to conduct bias detection and correction. So the DUTY to examine and mitigate bias comes from Art. 10(2)(f)-(g) and binds high-risk providers only, while Art. 4a is an enabling permission, not an obligation, and is not coded as a separate mandatory record. Must be read alongside the GDPR (Art. 1(2)(g) as amended is without prejudice to Art. 4a). APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128; OJ p. 123) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 13(1)-(3) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Transparency and provision of information to deployers
responsible_party: AI provider (information duty owed to deployers)
applicability: High-risk AI systems. The beneficiary of the information is the deployer, not end-users or affected persons. Transparency towards natural persons interacting with AI systems (e.g. chatbots, deepfakes) is a separate regime under Art. 50. Affected persons have a separate right to obtain explanations of individual decisions from the deployer (Art. 86, OJ p. 110).
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106). Deployers must use systems in accordance with the instructions for use (Art. 26(1); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37), with deployer breaches finable under Art. 99(4)(e).
exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately.
verification_notes: Binding requirement. Scope is B2B transparency (provider to deployer), not public disclosure; do not equate with general 'explainability to the public'. Art. 13(3)(b)(iv) requires explanation-relevant information only 'where applicable', so explainability is conditional rather than absolute. Cross-references: Art. 15 (accuracy metrics declared in instructions, Art. 15(3)), Art. 14 (oversight measures, Art. 13(3)(d)), Art. 12 (logs, Art. 13(3)(f)). Separate from Art. 50 transparency obligations (candidate for a later record). No M1 marker in Art. 13; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128; OJ p. 123) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). As of Nov 2026 the obligation is binding law but not yet applicable. document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 14(1)-(4) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Human oversight
responsible_party: AI provider (design obligation); AI deployer (implementation, via Art. 26(2))
applicability: High-risk AI systems. Additional two-person verification rule for remote biometric identification systems (Annex III point 1(a)), with an exception for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law deems it disproportionate (Art. 14(5)).
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106). Deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Art. 26(2); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37, OJ p. 68 for para. 2; unchanged by 2026/1744); breach finable under Art. 99(4)(e).
exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.
verification_notes: Binding requirement. Shared responsibility: Art. 14 itself places design duties on the provider (Art. 14(3)(a)-(b)), while the duty to actually staff oversight sits with deployers under Art. 26(2). Responsible party is therefore recorded as two actors; for responsibility analysis, count the provider as the primary duty-holder for this record and note Art. 26(2) as a possible separate deployer record. Classified as Accountability (human oversight is listed under that dimension in the codebook), although its stated aim (Art. 14(2)) is risk prevention, so there is a secondary link to Risk Assessment. The coded range is Art. 14(1)-(4); para. 5 (biometric two-person verification) appears only in applicability. No M1 marker in Art. 14; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128; OJ p. 123) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 15(1), (3)-(5) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
applicability: High-risk AI systems. The feedback-loop requirement (Art. 15(4), third subpara.) applies only to systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service.
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).
exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
verification_notes: Binding requirement, but the standard is open-textured ('appropriate level'; 'as resilient as possible'; measures 'where appropriate'), so in practice compliance will be specified through harmonised standards and benchmarks. Art. 15(2) is a separate INSTITUTIONAL duty on the Commission to encourage benchmarks and measurement methodologies. It is not counted in this record and could form a separate record (obligation_type = Institutional). Art. 15(3) (declared accuracy levels and metrics) is included in the coded range; it links to Transparency (Art. 13(3)(b)(ii)) but is not double counted. No M1 marker in Art. 15; wording unchanged. APPLICATION DATE: as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 113 (cons. p. 128; OJ p. 123) applies Chapter III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027 for systems classified under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 Aug 2028 for systems classified under Art. 6(1) and Annex I (originally 2 Aug 2026 and 2 Aug 2027 respectively). document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
article_or_section: Part 4 – Practical Guidelines for Industry & Regulators; 'Guidelines for industry', bullet 5 (transparency reports)
responsible_party: Developer and deployer ('any person involved in developing or deploying AI systems in India')
applicability: All developers and deployers of AI systems in India; no risk threshold or system category is defined. Elsewhere the Guidelines say that low-risk applications may need only basic commitments such as transparency reporting, while high-risk applications in sensitive sectors may need more (§2.4, PDF p. 30).
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision. The Guidelines rely on soft accountability mechanisms (public and peer scrutiny of transparency reports, self-certifications, internal policies, committee hearings, §2.5, PDF p. 33; peer monitoring and third-party audits, §2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance with these measures within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). Voluntary measures may later become mandatory baseline requirements enforced by regulators (§2.4, PDF p. 29).
exact_text: Publish transparency reports that evaluate the risk of harm to individuals and society in the Indian context.
verification_notes: Policy recommendation, not a directly enforceable obligation: Part 4 is introduced as what developers/deployers 'should be guided by'. Related provisions not double counted: Sutra 6 'Understandable by Design' (Part 1, PDF p. 15) and §2.5 'Transparency' about the AI value chain for regulators (PDF p. 35). COMPARISON NOTE: unlike EU AI Act Art. 13 (provider-to-deployer instructions), this is a public or regulator-facing risk-reporting expectation. Check whether MeitY has published the compliance schedule mentioned on PDF p. 33. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (information technology, data protection, consumer protection and statutory civil and criminal codes) can govern AI, 'given the current assessment of risks' (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
article_or_section: Part 2, §2.5 Accountability – Recommendations, bullet 2 (proportionate obligations across the AI value chain); read with 'Liability' (graded liability)
responsible_party: Government (MeitY and sectoral regulators) to clarify and impose obligations; the eventual duty-bearers would be developers, deployers and end-users
applicability: All entities in the AI value chain (developers, deployers, end-users). Obligations are to be scaled to function and risk; no thresholds are specified yet.
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision; the obligations themselves do not yet exist. Enforcement of existing laws is to be 'timely and consistent' (§2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). Part 3 Action Plan lists 'Develop clear liability regimes across the AI value chain' as a short-term action (PDF p. 40).
exact_text: Impose obligations for each of these entities that are proportionate to their function and the risk of harm
verification_notes: A recommendation that government should create future obligations; it imposes nothing itself. Record as Recommended with responsible party = Government. Do not count it as an obligation on developers until implemented in law. The RBI FREE-AI Committee's 'tolerant' stance on first-time aberrations is noted but not endorsed as a general rule; the Committee says the rule of law is paramount (PDF p. 34). Related, not double counted: Sutra 5 Accountability (PDF p. 15); grievance redressal recommendation 'Mandate grievance redressal mechanisms' (PDF p. 35), which is a candidate for a separate record. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (information technology, data protection, consumer protection and statutory civil and criminal codes) can govern AI, 'given the current assessment of risks' (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
article_or_section: Part 2, §2.4 Risk Mitigation – Recommendations, bullet 1 (India-specific risk assessment and classification framework)
responsible_party: Government (developing body not named in the provision; Action Plan says 'with sectoral inputs'; AISI's listed functions include risk analysis)
applicability: Economy-wide framework; it would determine which AI systems need which mitigation measures. No system categories exist yet.
enforcement_mechanism: Not applicable: this is a framework-building task, not a compliance duty. The linked AI incidents database (recommendation 2, PDF p. 32) is designed to encourage reporting 'without the threat of penalties' (PDF p. 29) and would feed evidence into the framework.
exact_text: Develop a risk assessment and classification framework that is customised for India’s local context, and accounts for risks to vulnerable groups.
verification_notes: Short-term action item in Part 3 ('Develop India-specific AI risk assessment and classification frameworks with sectoral inputs', PDF p. 40). Coded as Recommended, not Institutional, because the provision does not assign the task to a named institution. COMPARISON NOTE: contrast with EU AI Act, where risk classification is fixed in law (Art. 6, Annex III) and providers must run a risk management system (Art. 9). India has not yet defined risk tiers. Check whether the framework has been published since Nov 2025. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (information technology, data protection, consumer protection and statutory civil and criminal codes) can govern AI, 'given the current assessment of risks' (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
article_or_section: Part 2, §2.6 Institutions – B. AI Safety Institute (functions)
responsible_party: AI Safety Institute (IndiaAI Safety Institute), working with agencies and sectoral regulators
applicability: AI systems generally; no category of system is required to be submitted for testing, and no trigger for testing is defined. Standards bodies (BIS, TEC) are separately mapped to 'Standardising testing, assessment, evaluation and validation procedures' (PDF p. 43).
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified. AISI's role is research, testing and advice; the Guidelines give it no powers to compel testing or impose sanctions. It provides risk assessments and 'updates on industry compliance' to TPEC and AIGG (PDF p. 38).
exact_text: It should test and evaluate AI systems for risks and provide advice to policymakers and industry actors on issues of AI safety.
verification_notes: Institutional responsibility in a non-binding document: the guidelines describe AISI as 'recently established' (PDF p. 38) but its testing mandate here is advisory. There is no corresponding duty on developers to test or submit systems. ALTERNATIVE PROVISION not coded separately: §2.4 'Mitigating Loss of Control' (PDF p. 32) says that in critical sectors regular monitoring and testing, audit trails and reporting protocols 'should be implemented'. That is an industry-facing testing expectation and a candidate for a later record. COMPARISON NOTE: EU AI Act Art. 9(6)-(8) and Art. 15 place testing and robustness duties on providers; India places testing capacity in a state institution. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (information technology, data protection, consumer protection and statutory civil and criminal codes) can govern AI, 'given the current assessment of risks' (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). document: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (MeitY, IndiaAI Mission, 5 November 2025)
article_or_section: Part 2, §2.6 Institutions – whole-of-government approach, bullet 1 (sectoral regulators lead on enforcement)
responsible_party: Sectoral regulators and agencies (e.g. RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI, ICMR, NHA, ministries), with MeitY as nodal ministry and AIGG coordinating
applicability: AI applications falling within each regulator's existing statutory remit. Gaps between remits are left to AIGG to study ('regulatory gaps, and need for legal amendments', PDF p. 36).
enforcement_mechanism: Existing statutory powers of sectoral regulators under their own laws; no new AI-specific sanctions or enforcement powers are created. The institutional framework maps regulators to 'Enforcing applicable laws and regulations', 'Supervising compliance' and 'Handling grievances' (PDF pp. 42-43). AIGG is to 'issue guidelines to ensure that firms are held accountable for compliance with local laws' (PDF p. 36).
exact_text: The relevant sectoral agencies and regulators should take the lead in monitoring harms, providing guidance and enforcing regulations in their respective domains.
verification_notes: Institutional allocation of responsibility in non-binding guidance: the provision does not confer powers but points to powers regulators already have. Its legal force therefore depends on each sectoral statute. AIGG and TPEC are recommendations ('should be set up'); check whether they have since been constituted. Part 4 'Guidelines for regulators' (PDF p. 45) tell regulators to avoid compliance-heavy requirements such as mandatory approvals or licensing unless deemed necessary. That is relevant context for enforcement intensity; it is not coded separately. STATUS: the Guidelines are a drafting-committee report released by MeitY. They create no legal obligations. They expressly state that, at this stage, a separate AI law is not needed and that existing laws (information technology, data protection, consumer protection and statutory civil and criminal codes) can govern AI, 'given the current assessment of risks' (Overview, PDF p. 12 / printed p. 10). document: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (DSIT White Paper, CP 815, March 2023; amended version)
article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.3 A principles-based approach – Principle: Appropriate transparency and explainability
responsible_party: Regulatory authority (implementation through guidance); AI life cycle actors (may be asked by regulators to provide information)
applicability: All sectors, applied context-specifically by each regulator within its remit; the level of transparency is to be proportionate to the risk the AI system presents.
enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).
exact_text: AI systems should be appropriately transparent and explainable.
verification_notes: Non-statutory principle; it binds no one directly. Life cycle actors 'may be asked' to provide information, which is conditional on a regulator using existing powers. The White Paper consulted on, but did not adopt, a requirement that organisations disclose when they use AI (consultation Qs 1-2, PDF p. 38; wording corrected by the correction slip, PDF pp. 4-5). The explainability standard is qualified by context, risk and 'what is achievable given the state of the art' (PDF p. 35). STATUS: the White Paper is a policy proposal for consultation. Its principles are 'issued on a non-statutory basis and implemented by existing regulators' (para 11, PDF p. 12). It creates no legal obligations for businesses. Any binding effect comes from regulators' existing statutory powers. LATER DEVELOPMENTS: the Government response to consultation (CP 1019, 6 Feb 2024) kept this approach and should be coded as a separate document if used. It was published under the previous (2022-2024) government; secondary sources indicate no UK AI Act or statutory duty on regulators had been enacted by 2026. Verify on GOV.UK and legislation.gov.uk. document: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (DSIT White Paper, CP 815, March 2023; amended version)
article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.3 – Principle: Accountability and governance; read with §3.3.2 Government's role in addressing accountability across the life cycle (paras 80-83)
responsible_party: AI life cycle actors (organisations and individuals that research, design, develop, train, operate, deploy or use AI); regulatory authority (to set expectations)
applicability: All AI life cycle actors in all sectors; regulators decide which actors in the supply chain carry which expectations.
enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).
exact_text: Governance measures should be in place to ensure effective oversight of the supply and use of AI systems, with clear lines of accountability established across the AI life cycle.
verification_notes: Non-statutory principle. Para 80 (PDF p. 61) says legal responsibility for compliance should go to the actors 'best able to identify, assess and mitigate AI risks'. But para 83 (PDF p. 61) states the government is 'not proposing to intervene and make changes to life cycle accountability at this stage'. So no allocation of liability is made. COMPARISON NOTE: the EU AI Act allocates duties to named roles (provider, deployer, importer, distributor; Arts 16-26). The UK principle leaves allocation to regulators. Overlap: the principle mentions impact assessments as a way to identify risks early (Risk Assessment); not double counted. STATUS: the White Paper is a policy proposal for consultation. Its principles are 'issued on a non-statutory basis and implemented by existing regulators' (para 11, PDF p. 12). It creates no legal obligations for businesses. document: Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019; revised 8 November 2023 and 3 May 2024)
article_or_section: Section 1, Principle 1.3 Transparency and explainability (i)-(iv)
responsible_party: AI actors (Council 'CALLS ON all AI actors', para III); Adherent governments to promote and implement (para II)
applicability: All AI systems and AI actors, 'according to their respective roles'; qualified by context and 'consistent with the state of art'.
enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), practical implementation guidance (VIII(b)) and an information-exchange forum (VIII(c)) (see OECD005).
exact_text: AI Actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure regarding AI systems.
verification_notes: Non-binding principle; addressed both to governments and directly to AI actors. Point (iii) is limited to 'where feasible and useful'. The 2024 revision clarified the information AI actors should provide (Background, p. 4). BENCHMARK USE: compare (ii) awareness of interaction with EU AI Act Art. 50 and the UK consultation question on disclosure. Compare (iv) challenge with the UK contestability principle. STATUS: an OECD Council Recommendation adopted under Art. 5(b) of the OECD Convention (cited in the preamble, p. 7). Recommendations 'are not legally binding'; they represent a political commitment and an expectation that Adherents will do their best to implement them (About OECD Legal Instruments, p. 12). Not a country; use as a benchmark only. ADHERENCE: UK is an OECD Member (p. 12) and the EU adheres (OECD press release, 3 May 2024). A secondary tracker counts 49 Adherents as of Apr 2026. India is not an OECD Member; its adherence could not be confirmed (the Compendium page needs JavaScript). India is a founding GPAI member, which is not the same as formal adherence. article_or_section: Section 1, Principle 1.4 Robustness, security and safety, paragraphs (a)-(c)
